items.content_html:
A flaw was found in KubeVirt's virt-handler network cache handling. The writeToCachedFile function writes data to a launcher-rooted path using os.WriteFile and os.Chown without symlink protection. A user with access to the virt-launcher container can plant a symlink at the cache file path, causing virt-handler to follow it and overwrite an arbitrary host file with JSON content and change its ownership.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-13218
  • https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/CVE-2026-13218
  • https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2492654
  • https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/e63503d2f3a166f79f0891f8e1c3450eb39f88ac/pkg/network/cache/cache.go#L90-L103
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q3jc-42cq-33fj
items.title: [kubevirt.io/kubevirt] KubeVirt virt-handler network cache symlink vulnerability allows arbitrary host file overwrite

items.content_html:
A flaw was found in KubeVirt's downward metrics virtio-serial server. The server reads guest requests using textproto.Reader.ReadLine(), which buffers input indefinitely until a newline character is received, with no length limit or read deadline. A user with access to a VM guest that has the downward metrics virtio-serial device configured can write a continuous byte stream to the device, causing unbounded memory allocation in the virt-handler process until it is OOM-killed.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-13322
  • https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/CVE-2026-13322
  • https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2492681
  • https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/e63503d2f3a166f79f0891f8e1c3450eb39f88ac/pkg/downwardmetrics/virtio-serial/server.go#L240-L251
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6f2p-2qg2-qqch
items.title: [github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt] KubeVirt downward metrics virtio-serial server vulnerable to unbounded memory consumption

items.content_html:
Summary

The fix for CVE-2026-47735 (released 2026.06.1) is incomplete. It added a DuckDB sandbox (SET GLOBAL allowed_directories=[<storage root>]; SET GLOBAL enable_external_access=false) and an Arc SQL-layer denylist of the literal functions read_parquet( and arc_partition_agg(. The sandbox correctly blocks reads outside the storage root (OS files, http:// SSRF), but it allowlists the entire multi-tenant storage root, and the SQL denylist still misses the rest of the DuckDB I/O family the original advisory enumerated. As a result, any authenticated token — including one with permissions: [] — can read or enumerate every other database's data within the deployment, defeating RBAC.

Verified at HEAD c08b892 (v26.06.1-36, includes 26.06.2). Confirmed still live; no later commit blocks these functions.

Root cause (three composing gaps)

  1. Sandbox scope is the whole storage root, not the tenant. internal/database/sandbox.go:111 allowlists cfg.LocalStorageRoot (default storage.local_path=./data/arc). Every database lives under it — internal/storage/util.go:33 GetStoragePath => <base>/<database>/<measurement>/**/*.parquet. Any in-root path is sandbox-permitted regardless of which database owns it.
  2. RBAC never inspects table-valued functions. checkQueryPermissions (internal/api/query.go:1181) extracts table refs via extractTableReferences, which skips any name followed by ( as a function (internal/api/query.go:1116); with zero refs it returns allow (:1213-1216). So parquet_scan(...), glob(...), parquet_metadata(...), read_blob(...), read_csv_auto(...) are never authorization-checked.
  3. The SQL denylist matches only the literal spelling. userSQLReadParquetPattern (internal/api/query.go:2087) is \bread_parquet\s*\(. DuckDB's documented alias parquet_scan( is not matched, and read_csv_auto/read_json/read_text/read_blob/glob/parquet_metadata/parquet_schema are not blocked anywhere. The fix author documented this very threat at internal/api/query.go:2061-2064 (“a user scoped to db1.m1 could read /data/db2/secrets/**/*.parquet”) but blocked only the literal read_parquet(.

Exploit (authenticated, any token incl. permissions:[])

POST /api/v1/query
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json
{"sql": "SELECT * FROM parquet_scan('./data/arc/<victim-db>/<measurement>/**/*.parquet')"}
  • ValidateSQLRequest passes (parquet_scan( is not read_parquet(, not a dangerous keyword, single statement).
  • checkQueryPermissions extracts 0 table refs (it is a function call) and allows.
  • convertSQLToStoragePaths finds no read_parquet literal and no bare FROM measurement to rewrite, so the query passes through unchanged.
  • DuckDB runs parquet_scan('<root>/<victim-db>/...'); the path is inside allowed_directories, so the other database's rows are returned.

glob('./data/arc/**/*') enumerates every database/measurement/file; parquet_metadata(...)/parquet_schema(...) leak column names and per-column min/max value statistics; read_blob(...) returns raw file bytes. All operate within the allowlisted root.

Proof (poc/poc_sandbox_alias_bypass.py, poc/OUTPUT.txt)

Reproduces Arc's exact sandbox config (allowed_directories=[<root>], enable_external_access=false) on DuckDB 1.5.x (Arc pins duckdb-go-bindings 1.5.1) with a victim parquet written under the root:

[BLOCKED ] read_blob OUTSIDE root            -> Permission Error: Cannot access file ...
[EXECUTES] parquet_scan victim (read_parquet ALIAS) -> [('tenant-VICTIM-row', 42)]
[EXECUTES] glob enumerate every db under root -> [('.../data/arc/victim-db/secrets/f.parquet',)]
[EXECUTES] parquet_metadata victim           -> [('leaked','tenant-VICTIM-row','tenant-VICTIM-row'), ('v','42','42')]

The sandbox blocks escape (as designed) but permits every in-root cross-database read.

Impact

Cross-database / cross-tenant confidential read by any authenticated principal, including a least-privileged (permissions: []) token, on RBAC-enabled deployments. This is the same RBAC-bypass impact the original advisory described for read_parquet, still reachable via the alias and the unblocked I/O family. (Arc's SQLite token DB ./data/arc.db is a sibling of ./data/arc/ and is not in the allowlist, so it is not readable this way — the exposure is the time-series data of every database, plus its schema and value-range statistics.)

Remediation

Per-request scope the sandbox to the requesting token's authorized database path(s): allowed_directories = ['<base>/<authorized-db>/'], so the file layer cannot cross the RBAC boundary regardless of which function is used. Alternatively, replace the function-name denylist with a strict allowlist of permitted table functions (alias-resolved, reject all others). A denylist of literal spellings is structurally fragile — this is the second alias/family miss after the original audit.

References

  • https://github.com/Basekick-Labs/arc/security/advisories/GHSA-93cm-2v4m-c56c
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-55098
  • https://github.com/Basekick-Labs/arc/pull/495
  • https://github.com/Basekick-Labs/arc/commit/5dc8f53b70a3871b16b0cebf328f07c578af7a45
  • https://github.com/Basekick-Labs/arc/tree/v26.06.2
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-93cm-2v4m-c56c

items.content_html:
Summary

The RealIP middleware in go-chi/chi is vulnerable to IP spoofing because it blindly trusts the first (leftmost) element of the X-Forwarded-For HTTP header. This allows a remote attacker to bypass IP-based access control lists (ACLs) and rate-limiting mechanisms by providing a spoofed IP address in the header.

Details

In middleware/realip.go, the realIP function parses the X-Forwarded-For header and extracts the first comma-separated value:

func realIP(r *http.Request) string {
    // ...
    } else if xff := r.Header.Get(xForwardedFor); xff != "" {
        ip, _, _ = strings.Cut(xff, ",")
    }
    // ...
}

Standard practice for X-Forwarded-For is that each proxy appends the client's IP to the end of the list. However, since the client can also provide this header, the leftmost values are untrusted. A client can send a header like X-Forwarded-For: <spoofed_ip>, <actual_proxy_ip>, and go-chi/chi will treat <spoofed_ip> as the source of the request.

Proof of Concept (PoC)

The following code demonstrates how an attacker can bypass an IP-based restriction.

package main

import (
        "fmt"
        "net/http"
        "net/http/httptest"

        "github.com/go-chi/chi/v5"
        "github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
        r := chi.NewRouter()

        // Enable the vulnerable RealIP middleware
        r.Use(middleware.RealIP)

        // An endpoint that should be restricted to a specific administrator IP (1.2.3.4)
        r.Get("/admin/secret", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                clientIP := r.RemoteAddr
                fmt.Printf("[Server] Request received from IP: %s\n", clientIP)

                // Simulate IP-based access control
                if clientIP == "1.2.3.4" {
                        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
                        w.Write([]byte("CONFIDENTIAL: The secret code is 42\n"))
                } else {
                        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusForbidden)
                        w.Write([]byte("Access Denied: You are not an administrator.\n"))
                }
        })

        // --- Attack Simulation ---
        fmt.Println("--- PoC: IP Spoofing Attack on chi/middleware.RealIP ---")

        // 1. Normal Request (Should be denied)
        req1, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", "/admin/secret", nil)
        rr1 := httptest.NewRecorder()
        r.ServeHTTP(rr1, req1)
        fmt.Printf("[Client] Normal Request -> Status: %d, Body: %s", rr1.Code, rr1.Body.String())

        // 2. Spoofed Request (Using X-Forwarded-For)
        // Attacker claims to be '1.2.3.4'
        req2, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", "/admin/secret", nil)
        req2.Header.Set("X-Forwarded-For", "1.2.3.4, 5.6.7.8") // 5.6.7.8 is a fake proxy IP
        rr2 := httptest.NewRecorder()
        r.ServeHTTP(rr2, req2)
        fmt.Printf("[Client] Spoofed Request -> Status: %d, Body: %s", rr2.Code, rr2.Body.String())
}

Impact

An attacker can masquerade as any IP address. This can lead to:

  • Bypass of Authentication/Authorization: Accessing administrative panels or private APIs restricted by IP.
  • Rate Limiting Evasion: Circumbeting rate limiters that use RemoteAddr as a key.
  • Log Forgery: Causing incorrect IP addresses to be recorded in security logs.

CWE

  • CWE-290: Authentication Bypass by Spoofing
  • CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity

CVSS Score

  • CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.9 Moderate)

Affected Versions

  • github.com/go-chi/chi/v5 <= v5.2.1 (and all previous versions)

Recommendation

  1. Stop using middleware.RealIP if you cannot guarantee that the incoming request headers are from a trusted source and have been sanitized by a proxy.
  2. Implement a trust-based IP extraction mechanism that verifies the chain of proxies.
  3. Use the X-Forwarded-For header by traversing it from right to left and stopping at the first IP address that is not in your list of trusted proxies.

Suggested Fix

A secure implementation of RealIP should allow developers to specify a list of trusted proxy IP ranges (CIDRs). Below is a conceptual example of how to fix this by traversing the X-Forwarded-For header from right to left:

func GetClientIP(r *http.Request, trustedProxies []net.IPNet) string {
        xff := r.Header.Get("X-Forwarded-For")
        if xff == "" {
                return r.RemoteAddr
        }

        ips := strings.Split(xff, ",")
        // Traverse from right to left
        for i := len(ips) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
                ipStr := strings.TrimSpace(ips[i])
                ip := net.ParseIP(ipStr)
                if ip == nil {
                        continue
                }

                if !isTrustedProxy(ip, trustedProxies) {
                        return ipStr
                }
        }

        return r.RemoteAddr
}

func isTrustedProxy(ip net.IP, trustedProxies []net.IPNet) bool {
        for _, network := range trustedProxies {
                if network.Contains(ip) {
                        return true
                }
        }
        return false
}

By providing a configuration like middleware.RealIPWithConfig(Config{TrustedProxies: []string{"10.0.0.0/8"}}) , the middleware can safely identify the true client IP even in complex proxy environments.

References

  • https://github.com/go-chi/chi/security/advisories/GHSA-3fxj-6jh8-hvhx
  • https://github.com/go-chi/chi/pull/967
  • https://github.com/go-chi/chi/commit/3b171578ca44dfd75ca3c5cbddc7b44c600a7b49
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3fxj-6jh8-hvhx
items.title: [github.com/go-chi/chi/v5] chi Has an IP Spoofing Vulnerability in `middleware.RealIP`

items.content_html:
Impact

A remote Telegram user can write files to arbitrary paths inside an agent's persistent workspace volume (praktor-wk-<workspace>, mounted at /workspace/agent), escaping the documented uploads/ directory.

The attacker controls the Telegram document filename, which was concatenated into the destination path without sanitization (internal/telegram/bot.go, at both upload sites) and resolved with path.Join, which collapses ../ sequences. A filename like ../../../CLAUDE.md resolved to the root of the agent workspace volume, outside uploads/.

Because the agent workspace is the persistent working directory the Claude agent reads from and operates on across runs, writing outside uploads/ lets an attacker plant or overwrite files the agent later consumes — e.g. CLAUDE.md, agent instruction/skill/hook files, or other config under /workspace/agent. This turns a file upload into a stored injection into the agent's instruction/execution surface (CWE-22 path traversal escalating to stored instruction injection).

Reachability

By default the bot has no user allowlist (allow_from: [] means "allow all"), so the only precondition is that a user can message the bot. No authentication or prior privilege is required.

Affected versions

Through v0.9.0 (and HEAD 3902d29).

Patched versions

v0.9.1, containing PR #228.

Workarounds

Restrict telegram.allow_from to trusted user IDs to limit who can send uploads to the bot. Upgrading to v0.9.1 is the recommended fix.

Fix (defense in depth)

  • internal/telegram/bot.go: apply path.Base() to the attacker-controlled filename at both upload sites, stripping directory components and ...
  • internal/container/manager.go: WriteVolumeBytes now rejects any path that escapes /vol after path.Join, protecting future callers.

Credit

Reported privately by tonghuaroot, who provided a detailed root-cause analysis, a deployed end-to-end proof of concept against the real container.Manager, and fix verification.

References

  • https://github.com/mtzanidakis/praktor/security/advisories/GHSA-48v2-6jcm-fc99
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-62331
  • https://github.com/mtzanidakis/praktor/pull/228
  • https://github.com/mtzanidakis/praktor/commit/c3731eeda01c0b3ec1dbd13cccd5a147c3182141
  • https://github.com/mtzanidakis/praktor/releases/tag/v0.9.1

items.content_html:
Summary

Arc exposes GET /api/v1/logs without authentication even when authentication is enabled by default. The route is registered before the global Fiber authentication middleware, and the handler returns recent buffered application logs without performing its own authorization check.

Details

Arc applies the global auth middleware after calling server.RegisterRoutes():

  • cmd/arc/main.go:1598-1599 registers base routes via server.RegisterRoutes().
  • cmd/arc/main.go:1601-1618 configures and installs auth.NewMiddleware(...) later.

server.RegisterRoutes() registers GET /api/v1/logs as a base route:

  • internal/api/server.go:164-183 registers base health, metrics, and logs routes, including s.app.Get("/api/v1/logs", s.logsHandler).

The logs handler returns buffered logs without checking authentication or authorization:

  • internal/api/server.go:537-567 parses limit, level, and since_minutes, reads logger.GetBuffer().GetRecent(...), and returns JSON.
  • internal/logger/buffer.go:9-16 defines log entries returned to callers: timestamp, level, component, message, and caller.
  • internal/logger/buffer.go:33-39 creates a global log buffer holding the last 10,000 entries.
  • internal/api/server.go:540-558 permits up to limit=1000 and since_minutes=1440 in one unauthenticated request.

Authentication is enabled by default and /api/v1/logs is not listed as a public route:

  • internal/config/config.go:841-843 defaults auth to enabled.
  • internal/auth/middleware.go:29-41 public defaults are /health, /ready, /api/v1/auth/verify, and /metrics prefix; /api/v1/logs is not public.

However, Fiber route/middleware order makes the later middleware ineffective for an earlier exact route. Local verification against Fiber v2.52.13 showed a route registered before app.Use(...) returns 200 and the later middleware is not reached. Fiber’s router walks routes in declaration order and stops after the first matching route unless the handler calls c.Next(); logsHandler does not call c.Next().

Proof of concept

Safe local reproduction only; do not scan external infrastructure.

  1. Start Arc with default authentication enabled.
  2. Request logs without an Authorization header or x-api-key header:
curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/logs?limit=1000&since_minutes=1440'

Expected vulnerable result:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"timestamp":"...","count":...,"logs":[...]}
  1. Compare with a protected endpoint without credentials:
curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/auth/tokens'

Expected protected result:

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized

This demonstrates that default auth is active while /api/v1/logs bypasses it due to registration order.

Impact

An unauthenticated network attacker can retrieve recent application logs. Depending on deployment and log level, logs can disclose operational metadata such as component names, internal paths, database/measurement names, node identifiers, caller locations, request outcomes, and error details. This can assist further attacks and may expose sensitive data if any deployment logs secrets or user-controlled confidential data.

The audit did not confirm that the bootstrap admin token banner is captured by this endpoint; that banner is printed with fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, ...), while this endpoint reads the zerolog-backed application buffer.

Workarounds

Until patched, operators can restrict access to /api/v1/logs at a reverse proxy, firewall, ingress policy, or service mesh. If the endpoint is not needed, block it entirely.

Suggested fix

  • Move /api/v1/logs registration after global auth middleware and require an authenticated administrator; or
  • Add explicit route-level middleware: auth.RequireAdmin(authManager) for /api/v1/logs; and
  • Add a regression test that unauthenticated requests to /api/v1/logs return 401/403 while /health and /ready remain public.

References / evidence

  • cmd/arc/main.go:1598-1618
  • internal/api/server.go:164-183
  • internal/api/server.go:537-567
  • internal/auth/middleware.go:29-41
  • internal/config/config.go:841-843
  • internal/logger/buffer.go:9-16
  • internal/logger/buffer.go:33-39

References

  • https://github.com/Basekick-Labs/arc/security/advisories/GHSA-m3qr-fvp4-78xj
  • https://github.com/Basekick-Labs/arc/pull/506
  • https://github.com/Basekick-Labs/arc/commit/bb7d9761ad9801e93837762ff7d37460f1df19dd
  • https://github.com/Basekick-Labs/arc/releases/tag/v26.06.2
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m3qr-fvp4-78xj

items.content_html:
Impact

Podman v4.4.0 added a feature where container checkpoints (from the podman container checkpoint command) could be distributed via OCI registry, and pulled from that registry and run via the podman run command. This allowed easy transfer of checkpoints between systems. However, checkpoints allow complete control of how the container is created - including full control of the container sandbox. When podman run detects a checkpoint, it will silently ignore all user input regarding how the container should be created - for example, podman run --cap-drop=ALL on an image that is determined to be a checkpoint will ignore --cap-drop=all and use the set of capabilities specified by the checkpoint image instead, which could include all capabilities. Podman identifies checkpoint images by looking for an annotation, io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name. If this annotation is set, the image is treated as a checkpoint. Conflating container images and checkpoints in podman run allows inherently insecure behavior as the image can now control how it is executed. The Podman Maintainers have determined that the safest course of action is to remove this functionality.

Patch

The commit introducing this functionality was reverted.

3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669 c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627 fa6cef22c2baf3987b581c673bb416ef0585daf7 (main) ea9243e04d1db3886dc3a51ee3300ffb547cfc02 450c64426dbcff1097d3c7911d791101e3d16f4c 2d05a7c61f022d4f24980ea6d307fa53da2b8692 (v6.1) 7728ba0a90094408ad9078e36c3622a651d49616 24706290d5c974f078d8ca284026802515f28e92 29c8c6e50607df7a7d735ace09ff0ea099c0b3e0 (v5.8)

Workarounds

Images being pulled should be scanned for the io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name annotation, and rejected if it is present. Podman does not presently have the ability to perform this scanning and rejection automatically.

Also not that rootless containers are not affected as they do not support checkpoint/restore at all currently.

Credits

This vulnerability was discovered by ADA Logics Ltd using Anthropic's Claude models.

References

  • https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/security/advisories/GHSA-2cvf-wqm6-wr9g

  • https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/commit/3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669
  • https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/commit/450c64426dbcff1097d3c7911d791101e3d16f4c
  • https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/commit/7728ba0a90094408ad9078e36c3622a651d49616
  • https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/commit/c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627
  • https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/commit/ea9243e04d1db3886dc3a51ee3300ffb547cfc02
  • https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/releases/tag/v5.8.8

items.content_html:
Impact

Podman v4.4.0 added a feature where container checkpoints (from the podman container checkpoint command) could be distributed via OCI registry, and pulled from that registry and run via the podman run command. This allowed easy transfer of checkpoints between systems. However, checkpoints allow complete control of how the container is created - including full control of the container sandbox. When podman run detects a checkpoint, it will silently ignore all user input regarding how the container should be created - for example, podman run --cap-drop=ALL on an image that is determined to be a checkpoint will ignore --cap-drop=all and use the set of capabilities specified by the checkpoint image instead, which could include all capabilities. Podman identifies checkpoint images by looking for an annotation, io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name. If this annotation is set, the image is treated as a checkpoint. Conflating container images and checkpoints in podman run allows inherently insecure behavior as the image can now control how it is executed. The Podman Maintainers have determined that the safest course of action is to remove this functionality.

Patch

The commit introducing this functionality was reverted.

3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669 c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627 fa6cef22c2baf3987b581c673bb416ef0585daf7 (main) ea9243e04d1db3886dc3a51ee3300ffb547cfc02 450c64426dbcff1097d3c7911d791101e3d16f4c 2d05a7c61f022d4f24980ea6d307fa53da2b8692 (v6.1) 7728ba0a90094408ad9078e36c3622a651d49616 24706290d5c974f078d8ca284026802515f28e92 29c8c6e50607df7a7d735ace09ff0ea099c0b3e0 (v5.8)

Workarounds

Images being pulled should be scanned for the io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name annotation, and rejected if it is present. Podman does not presently have the ability to perform this scanning and rejection automatically.

Also not that rootless containers are not affected as they do not support checkpoint/restore at all currently.

Credits

This vulnerability was discovered by ADA Logics Ltd using Anthropic's Claude models.

Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server decompresses uploaded pipeline archives without adequately bounding expanded data in affected versions. A small ZIP or gzip-compressed tar archive can consume disproportionately large amounts of memory while the server locates or reads the pipeline file, potentially exhausting API-server resources and interrupting service.

Multipart pipeline and pipeline-version upload processing decompresses the archive before namespace authorization, so a caller who can reach those endpoints does not need a successful pipeline-create authorization decision to trigger the issue. External authentication and network controls can restrict reachability. URL-import handlers authorize before fetching and decompressing a remote archive.

The amount of expansion needed to exhaust memory depends on deployment resource limits and concurrent activity; no particular archive is guaranteed to crash every deployment.

Remediation

Upgrade the API server to Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

PR #14171 bounds compressed input and extracted pipeline data. PR #14186 strengthens the total tar traversal budget, including metadata and skipped entries. The 2.18 release also includes configurable upload and specification limits; operators should review the shipped settings and resource budget. These controls address pipeline archive amplification and do not establish general HTTP-body, temporary-disk, concurrency, or CPU limits.

Until upgrading, restrict access to upload and import endpoints and apply deployment-level request and resource controls. A compressed upload-size limit alone does not prevent decompression amplification. Regression tests cover compressed input, selected-entry boundaries, and tar traversal budgets; no deployed-server OOM test was performed for this assessment.

Credit

bugbunny.ai discovered and reported the issue. Ayush Gupta (@Ayush-kathil) authored the archive fixes in #14171 and #14186, with Jeff Spahr (@jeffspahr) contributing regression coverage to #14171.

@BrianWillows later submitted a mixed report that included source analysis of pipeline-archive decompression.

Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

For live logs, the vulnerable handler also accepts the supplied node ID as a pod name in the run's namespace without verifying that the pod belongs to the run. Depending on the API server's pod-log permissions, a known run ID can therefore permit reading the main container logs of an unrelated pod in that namespace. Logs may contain sensitive workload data or credentials.

The affected handler does not authenticate the request itself. An external authentication gate or network policy can restrict reachability; public ingress exposure and unauthenticated enumeration of run IDs are not assumed.

Remediation

Upgrade the API server to Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

PR #13684 authorizes the caller with the readLog verb before retrieving live or archived logs. For live logs, it also verifies that the pod's pipeline/runid label matches the requested run. Custom Kubernetes roles must grant readLog on runs in the pipelines.kubeflow.org API group; the bundled viewer and editor roles include it. Shared read access alone does not grant log access.

Until upgrading, restrict access to the backend log endpoint. Focused regression tests cover authorization denial, HTTP identity propagation, pod/run mismatch, archive retrieval, and cancellation; no new deployed-cluster end-to-end test was performed for this assessment.

Credit

bugbunny.ai discovered and reported the issue. Nayyar (@naruto-lgtm) authored the fix in #13684.

@patchmyday, @thesecguy45, @VitoCrl, @Grg0rry, @arpitjain099, and @BrianWillows made later submissions concerning the run-log authorization gap. MUTEDCYBERSECURITY S.L. separately reported a synthetic two-tenant reproduction, including the unrelated-pod log path.

items.content_html:
Summary

In v2.52.1 and v2.52.2 the CORS middleware matched a wildcard origin such as https://*.example.com by suffix only, without a dot boundary and without comparing the scheme. Any origin whose host ends with the base domain, for example https://evil-example.com or http://notexample.com, was reflected in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true when AllowCredentials is enabled.

v2.52.3 replaced the matcher (#2915) and is not affected. The report was filed against v2.52.15, where the dot boundary holds; see "Other versions" below.

Details

v2.52.1 introduced validateDomain in middleware/cors/utils.go (f0cd3b44, part of the fix for GHSA-fmg4-x8pw-hjhg). It strips scheme and port from both sides and then checks only the suffix, with trimmedPattern = "example.com", so the character before the suffix is never checked:

if strings.HasPrefix(normalizedPattern, "*.") {
    trimmedPattern := normalizedPattern[2:]
    if strings.HasSuffix(normalizedDomain, trimmedPattern) {
        if normalizedDomain != trimmedPattern {
            if strings.TrimSuffix(normalizedDomain, trimmedPattern) != "" {
                return true
            }
        }
    }
}

v2.52.3 (1aac6f61, #2915) replaced it with a scheme-aware prefix/suffix split that keeps the leading dot in the suffix (.example.com).

Proof of concept

app := fiber.New()
app.Use(cors.New(cors.Config{
    AllowOrigins:     "https://*.example.com",
    AllowCredentials: true,
}))
app.Get("/", func(c *fiber.Ctx) error { return c.SendString("secret") })

Request with Origin: https://evil-example.com, as a GET and as a preflight (OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method: GET):

Version https://evil-example.com http://evil-example.com
v2.52.0 not allowed not allowed
v2.52.1, v2.52.2 reflected, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true reflected, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
v2.52.3 to v2.52.16 not allowed not allowed

Impact

An app that configures a wildcard-subdomain AllowOrigins with AllowCredentials: true lets any page on a domain that ends with the base domain (for example notexample.com for *.example.com) read authenticated responses cross-origin. Fixed in v2.52.3; upgrade to the latest v2 release.

Other versions

All v2 releases before v2.52.16 also accepted origins with empty labels (https://.example.com, https://a..example.com), and v2.52.3 to v2.52.15 mis-parsed a wildcard entry after a comma and a space ("https://a.com, https://*.example.com"). No registrable domain produces such an origin, so these are hardening rather than part of this advisory. They are fixed in v2.52.16 (#4792).

References

  • https://github.com/gofiber/fiber/security/advisories/GHSA-g5jq-qmqr-qrwf
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119285
  • https://github.com/gofiber/fiber/pull/2915
  • https://github.com/gofiber/fiber/commit/1aac6f618b6bd3e159d2449acb4232a2170b976b
  • https://github.com/gofiber/fiber/releases/tag/v2.52.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g5jq-qmqr-qrwf

items.content_html:
Summary

The ICO loader allocates data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN bytes after reading a 32-bit attacker-controlled data_size. For data_size > UINT32_MAX - BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN, the addition wraps before allocation. imgproxy then writes the ICO prefix and reads up to the original declared size starting 14 bytes into the undersized allocation. A network client can turn this heap overflow into remote denial of service or remote code execution.

Technical details

The vulnerable path is in vips/icoload.c at commit f4fedbb:

uint32_t data_size = GUINT32_FROM_LE(largest_image_header.data_size);

VipsPel *data = (VipsPel *) VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN);
void *actual_data = data + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN;

if (vips_foreign_load_read_full(ico->source, actual_data, data_size) <= 0) {
  vips_error("vips_foreign_load_ico_header", "unable to read ICO image data from the source");
  return -1;
}

The crafted directory entry contains:

data_size       = 0xfffffff5 (4294967285)
data_offset     = 22
BMP header size = 14
32-bit result   = (0xfffffff5 + 14) mod 2^32 = 3

The allocation is therefore three bytes. actual_data points 14 bytes after the allocation base. The fixture contains 64 bytes after the ICO header, so the source callback copies those 64 bytes to an invalid destination before it can report that the declared multi-gigabyte payload is incomplete.

The complete source-to-sink path is:

  1. Attacker-controlled bytes begin with the ICO magic 00 00 01 00.
  2. imgproxy identifies the source as ICO and dispatches it to vips_icoload_source_go.
  3. vips_foreign_load_ico_header reads the attacker-controlled data_size.
  4. The 32-bit addition wraps, and VIPS_MALLOC receives the value three.
  5. vips_foreign_load_read_full passes the original data_size to the Go source callback.
  6. The callback writes the available source bytes through the invalid pointer, corrupting the process heap.

Impact

A crafted image can terminate the imgproxy process handling it or potentially lead to remote code execution due to heap corruption.

References

  • https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/security/advisories/GHSA-hff9-5pqw-6w9f
  • https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/commit/a821b6a4cb07a1bf2bb9077431d1c1e734d79917
  • https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/releases/tag/v4.0.16
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hff9-5pqw-6w9f

items.content_html:
Summary

Out-of-bounds heap write in imgproxy's ICO loader (vips/icoload.c): when the ICO entry's image data buffer is small, the loader's BMP-header-reconstruction writes land past the allocation, corrupting the size field of the following heap chunk. The worker then aborts deterministically (glibc munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer → SIGABRT → Go panic, exit code 2).

Details

In vips_foreign_load_ico_header in vips/icoload.c, after the ICO entry's image data is read into a heap buffer of data_size + 14 bytes, the loader reconstructs a BMP file header in front of it using fields read from the ICO's internal BITMAPINFOHEADER:

uint32_t num_colors = GUINT32_FROM_LE(*(uint32_t *) (actual_data + 32));  // unvalidated
uint16_t bpp        = GUINT16_FROM_LE(*(uint16_t *) (actual_data + 14));  // unvalidated

if ((num_colors == 0) && (bpp <= 8))
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * (1 << bpp);
else
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * num_colors;

int32_t height = GINT32_FROM_LE(*(int32_t *) (actual_data + 8));  // readable past the buffer
height = height / 2;

With a crafted entry declaring a tiny data_size (e.g. 1 byte), all of these reads (offsets +8, +14, +32) go past the allocation, and the reconstructed-header writes land past the end of the buffer — specifically a 32-bit height/2-derived value at alloc+22..+25, overwriting the LSBs of the size field of the physically following heap chunk. The corrupted size is always original_size >> 1 and, in cgo thread arenas, the NON_MAIN_ARENA bit lands in the IS_MMAPPED position of the corrupted word such that the next free() of the victim deterministically takes glibc's munmap_chunk() abort path, killing the worker. Depending on heap state, the worker returns 500 for the triggering request and aborts on the corrupted chunk's free; in observed production geometry it dies on the same request (exit code 2).

PoC

# make_ico_oob.py — generates the exact 23-byte OOB-write trigger.
# Byte-identical to the checksummed, production-verified file:
#   ico-oob.ico  sha256 075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1
import struct, hashlib

hdr = struct.pack('<HHH', 0, 1, 1)  # reserved, type=ICO, count=1
# 16x16, 0 colors, 0 reserved, 1 plane, 32 bpp, data_size=1, data_offset=0x16.
# The tiny data_size (1) makes the loader's BMPINFOHEADER field reads
# (data+8/+14/+32) and header-reconstruction writes go past the 1+14=15-byte
# allocation.
entry = struct.pack('<BBBBHHII', 16, 16, 0, 0, 1, 32, 1, 0x16)
data = b'\xAA'  # the single declared image byte
blob = hdr + entry + data
assert hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() == \
    '075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1'
open('ico-oob.ico', 'wb').write(blob)
print(f"ico-oob.ico: {len(blob)} bytes [VERIFIED]")

# imgproxy v4.0.15 with local file sources enabled:
#   IMGPROXY_ENABLE_LOCAL_FILES=true IMGPROXY_LOCAL_FILESYSTEM_ROOT=/ imgproxy
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/ico-oob.ico@png"
# → request fails at transport level (connection reset / empty reply) or
#   HTTP 500; worker dies: munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer → SIGABRT →
#   Go panic dump → exit code 2. One request, one dead worker.

curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/normal.ico@png"
# → HTTP 200, valid thumbnail (control)

Impact

Out-of-bounds write; demonstrated impact is denial of service (worker crash per crafted request). Any imgproxy deployment from the 3.3.x ICO-support series through v4.0.15 (latest at time of report) that processes attacker-supplied images.
